fatal_errors: The hypothesis identifies generic coherent-interface HEA multilayers, whereas the target transition occurs specifically in the semicoherent, 16 nm-period FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayer.
It replaces room-temperature nanoindentation creep with unspecified high-temperature testing and therefore assigns the wrong experimental regime.
It does not reconstruct modulation-period control or the comparison among coherent M8, semicoherent M16, and grain-boundary-dominated M32/M80 coatings.
It provides no causal mechanism involving misfit-dislocation blocking, pileup, localized stress, proposed interfacial amorphization, or enhanced atomic migration/interface slip.
The cited evidence concerns unrelated bulk or additively manufactured HEAs and does not support interface-coherency-dependent creep in the studied multilayers.
explanation: The response recognizes that interface coherency may govern a transition between diffusion- and dislocation-mediated creep, so it has limited topical alignment. However, it misses the central result: an approximately 1 μm-thick Al-Cr-Fe-Ni FCC/BCC multilayer with a 16 nm modulation period and semicoherent interfaces showed the transition and strongest reported room-temperature creep resistance. Coherent M8 and grain-boundary-dominated M32/M80 instead exhibited predominantly dislocation-mediated creep. The proposed high-temperature in-situ microscopy does not reconstruct the actual room-temperature, 5 mN nanoindentation protocol, and the generic correlation-based falsification rule would not distinguish the proposed mechanisms. None of the supplied citations validates the material-specific claim.
